A1.justification: I support the specification's rejection of Absalon data and commitment to fairness, but with a critical reservation: it lacks an explicit 'human-in-the-loop' safeguard before outreach. While the model avoids behavioral surveillance, automated flags based on grades alone can still misinterpret structural barriers as individual failure without advisor intervention. I would only endorse this if every flag requires human review to contextualize data (e.g., considering work or disability) before contacting a student. Without this step, even 'safe' data risks stigmatizing vulnerable students by reducing their complex struggles to simple metrics.

A2.justification: I support this model only if we enforce two critical safeguards: first, 'Absalon' data must remain strictly internal for advisor review and never trigger automated student contact; second, any flag based on behavioral or sensitive data requires human verification before outreach. The specification correctly prioritizes explainability and fairness, but without a strict 'human-in-the-loop' mechanism to prevent algorithmic misinterpretation of diverse learning styles as failure, the system risks stigmatizing vulnerable students rather than helping them.

A3.justification: I support this model only with the strict reservation that 'human-in-the-loop' verification is mandatory before any personalized contact occurs, especially when Absalon data or sensitive indicators are involved without a clear improvement threshold. Furthermore, there must be an explicit legal safeguard against 'mission creep,' ensuring these predictive records can never be used for disciplinary actions or performance reviews. Without these operational safeguards and student consent mechanisms, even this carefully balanced specification risks eroding the trust required for students to accept help.
